screens.title: Elastic Load Balancing: ALB, NLB, GWLB
screens.narratorSegment: Elastic Load Balancing is the front door for your application. At its core it distributes incoming traffic across multiple targets to increase fault tolerance and scalability. The Application Load Balancer operates at the application layer and is purpose-built for HTTP and HTTPS workloads. Use it when you need host-, path-, or header-based routing and when integrating with containers or microservices. The Network Load Balancer works at the transport layer for TCP, UDP, or TLS traffic and shines when extreme performance and static IP addresses are required. It is ideal for high-throughput, low-latency services. The Gateway Load Balancer is a specialized option for deploying third-party virtual appliances such as firewalls or intrusion detection systems; it helps insert and scale network appliances transparently. A common misconception is thinking ALB is always the best choice because it has advanced routing; instead match the layer and protocol to your workload. For example, a web application with URL-based routing and AWS WAF should use ALB. A high-frequency trading gateway requiring microsecond latency should consider NLB and placement of instances in a cluster placement group. Remember that the choice impacts routing, health checks, and how target registration works.

keyIdea.text: Match the load balancer to the OSI layer and your functional needs: ALB for Layer 7 routing, NLB for Layer 4 performance, GWLB for network appliances.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › ELB Types
Compare ELB types
Choose by protocol, performance, and appliance needs
Application Load Balancer (ALB)
Layer 7 routing for HTTP/HTTPS with host and path rules; integrates with containers and WAF.
Network Load Balancer (NLB)
Layer 4 performance for TCP/UDP/TLS, supports static IPs and very high throughput with low latency.
Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB)
Layer 3 gateway for inserting and scaling virtual network appliances like firewalls.
Key Takeaway

Select by protocol and operational need: routing features for ALB, throughput for NLB, appliance insertion for GWLB.

Concrete examples
ALB: Host-based routing directs api.example.com to the API service and www.example.com to the web service. Integrate AWS WAF for request filtering.
NLB: Expose a trading gateway that requires TLS termination and stable IPs, handling millions of small requests with low latency.
GWLB: Chain a firewall appliance for deep packet inspection in front of your VPC subnets.
Common Mistake

Assuming ALB covers all cases. If your app needs Layer 4 performance or static IPs, ALB is not the best fit.

screens.title: Auto Scaling Groups (ASG)
screens.narratorSegment: An Auto Scaling Group is a control plane construct that ensures a specified number of healthy EC2 instances are running. It automates instance lifecycle actions: launching new instances when demand increases or when health checks fail, and terminating instances when demand drops. To configure an ASG you provide a launch template that defines AMI, instance type, security groups, and user data. You also set desired, minimum, and maximum capacities so the group knows its safe operating window. ASGs integrate with CloudWatch alarms to trigger scaling actions and with load balancers to register targets and use ELB health checks. A practical example: set desired capacity to two and minimum to one so your application can tolerate a single instance failure while keeping cost under control. A misconception is treating ASG as purely reactive; with target tracking it behaves proactively to maintain metrics like average C P U. Proper health checks and cooldowns are essential; without them an ASG can rapidly spawn and kill instances, a condition called flapping. Think of ASG as an automated steward of your compute capacity. Auto Scaling Groups (ASG) means asg keeps a fleet at desired size and manages launches/terminations based on capacity and policy rules.. In practical terms, ensure availability by maintaining a desired fleet size. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Lifecycle management for a group of EC2 instances
Launch template

screens.title: Launch Templates & User Data
screens.narratorSegment: A launch template centralizes the configuration that an ASG uses when launching EC2 instances. It includes the AMI, instance type, security groups, and user data. User data is a script executed during the first boot and is commonly used to install packages, start services, and render configuration files. This is essential for immutable infrastructure: every time an instance launches it runs the same bootstrap steps. For example, a user data script can install Nginx and write an index page that displays the instance hostname, making it easy to validate ELB routing. A common misconception is embedding secrets in user data; instead use IAM roles or a secrets service. In the visual code panel you'll see a sample user data script that updates the package manager, installs Nginx, enables the service, and writes a simple H T M L file with the instance's hostname. When building launch templates, pin AMI IDs to stable versions and keep security groups minimal for least privilege. This pattern enables automatic, consistent instance configuration and faster recovery when ASG replaces instances. Launch Templates & User Data means use a launch template with user data to ensure each instance boots into the same, production-ready state automatically.. In practical terms, automate instance setup at boot with reproducible templates. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Launch Templates
User data example
A reproducible bootstrap script used in a launch template
<!-- User data script for Amazon Linux -->
#!/bin/bash
sudo yum update -y
sudo yum install -y nginx
sudo systemctl start nginx
sudo systemctl enable nginx
echo "<h1>Hello from $(hostname -f)</h1>" | sudo tee /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html
Note: the script runs once at first boot. Use instance roles instead of inline secrets.
Why this matters
Automates software install and service start so new instances are ready to serve traffic without manual steps.
Helps validate that ASG launches and ALB routing work by surfacing the hostname per instance.
Supports immutable infrastructure practices: replace instances instead of patching in place.
Pro tip
Keep user data idempotent and avoid embedding credentials. Use tagged AMIs and versioned scripts for predictable rollouts.

screens.title: Scaling Policies: Simple, Step, and Target Tracking
screens.narratorSegment: Scaling policies define the rules an Auto Scaling Group follows when adjusting capacity. A simple scaling policy reacts to a single alarm: when a metric crosses a threshold, the ASG performs a fixed scaling action, such as adding two instances. Step scaling refines this by mapping different threshold ranges to different actions — for example, add one instance when C P U exceeds 60 percent, add three when it exceeds 80 percent. Target tracking is the most hands-off and commonly recommended approach: you pick a metric and a desired target, such as average C P U at 60 percent, and the ASG automatically adjusts capacity to maintain that target. This reduces manual tuning and complexity. However, target tracking requires choosing a metric that accurately reflects application load. Watch for flapping if you omit cooldowns or if your metric is noisy; step policies can be useful when you need aggressive responses to large spikes. A good practice is to use target tracking for steady-state metrics and step policies for predictable large-scale events. Always test in a staging environment and monitor CloudWatch metrics to validate policy behavior.

keyIdea.text: Use target tracking for stable, metric-driven autoscaling; use step scaling for multi-threshold reactions; use simple scaling for basic single-threshold needs.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Scaling Policies
Policy types defined
How the ASG changes capacity
Simple scaling
One alarm triggers one scaling action, e.g., add 2 instances when CPU > 70%.
Step scaling
Different breach levels map to different adjustments, enabling graduated responses.
Target tracking
ASG keeps a metric near a target value, automatically calculating required capacity changes.
When to use each

Target tracking for predictable goals, step for variable spikes, simple for quick, manual thresholds.

Concrete example
Target tracking: set Average CPU target = 60. ASG will add or remove instances to keep average near 60%.
Step scaling: add 1 instance if CPU > 60, add 3 if CPU > 80 to react faster under heavy load.
Common mistake
Not setting proper cooldowns or using a noisy metric causes oscillation; choose stable signals and test thoroughly.

screens.title: ASG & CloudWatch Integration
screens.narratorSegment: Auto Scaling reacts to CloudWatch alarms which observe metrics from instances and load balancers. An alarm evaluates a metric over a period and triggers scaling actions when a threshold is breached. Health checks belonging to ELB or EC2 ensure that instances that fail to respond are marked unhealthy and replaced. A typical flow: CloudWatch alarm detects sustained high C P U, ASG scales out by launching instances using the launch template, the new instances run user data and register with the target group, and ELB health checks confirm readiness before routing traffic. If you forget to use ELB health checks, the ASG may mark an instance healthy before it is actually serving traffic. Another failure mode is missing IAM permissions for instances to reach configuration endpoints or to fetch secrets, which prevents bootstrapping. When designing alarms, pick evaluation periods and datapoints that smooth short spikes and set cooldowns so new instances have time to initialize. This flow minimizes false positives and ensures scaling decisions are effective and safe. ASG & CloudWatch Integration means cloudwatch alarms trigger asg actions; health checks verify readiness and cooldowns prevent rapid flapping.. In practical terms, how alarms drive scaling actions and the role of health checks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › ASG & CloudWatch
Typical scaling flow
Alarms, scaling, bootstrapping, and health validation
1. Observe
CloudWatch evaluates metrics and triggers an alarm on sustained breaches.
2. Act
ASG scales according to the policy and launch template to add or remove capacity.
3. Verify
ELB health checks ensure only ready instances receive traffic; unhealthy ones are replaced.
Example configuration
CloudWatch alarm: Average CPU > 70 over 5 minutes → triggers target tracking or step policy.
ELB health path: / returns 200; instance only considered healthy after passing checks.
Common Mistake
Using a very short evaluation period and no cooldown leads to scaling on transient spikes. Smooth metrics and give instances time to initialize.

screens.title: EC2 Placement Groups
screens.narratorSegment: Placement groups influence how EC2 instances are placed on underlying hardware to meet specific workload requirements. A Cluster placement group packs instances closely in a single Availability Zone to achieve low network latency and high throughput, which is valuable for high-performance computing. A Spread placement group distributes instances across distinct hardware to minimize correlated failures; each instance runs on different racks, making this a good choice for critical single-instance services like primary databases. Partition placement groups divide the fleet into partitions that isolate groups of instances from each other; instances in different partitions do not share underlying hardware, providing fault isolation useful for distributed systems like Cassandra, HDFS, or Kafka. A common misconception is that placement groups increase availability across AZs; they are confined to AZs, so you must combine them with multi-AZ architectures for full AZ-level resilience. Choose cluster for performance, spread for individual instance resilience, and partition for large distributed clusters needing partition-wise isolation. EC2 Placement Groups means use cluster for low latency and throughput, spread to reduce correlated hardware failure, partition for large-scale isolation across partitions.. In practical terms, cluster, spread, and partition explained with use cases. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Placement Groups
Cluster
Packs instances close together in one AZ for ultra-low latency and high network throughput. Ideal for HPC.
Use when inter-node network performance dominates application behavior.
Spread
Places each instance on distinct underlying hardware to reduce correlated failures. Good for critical single-instance services.
Use for primary databases or critical nodes that must avoid hardware co-location.
Partition
Divides instances into partitions that do not share underlying hardware, providing isolation for large distributed systems.
Use for distributed data systems that can tolerate partition-level failures.
Why this matters

Placement groups let you tune for latency, throughput, or hardware independence. Combine with multi-AZ architecture to avoid AZ-level single points of failure.

screens.title: Activity: Create ALB, Launch Template, and ASG
screens.narratorSegment: This activity ties the concepts together in a repeatable sequence. First, create an Application Load Balancer configured as internet-facing with listeners on HTTP:80, and register a target group using instances as targets. Choose at least two subnets across AZs to improve availability. Second, create a launch template named web-server-template with an Amazon Linux AMI, t2. micro instance type, and a security group that allows HTTP from the ALB and SSH from your IP. Include user data that installs Nginx and writes an index page showing the hostname. Third, create an Auto Scaling Group that uses the launch template, attaches to the ALB target group, and sets desired=2, min=1, max=4. Use a target tracking scaling policy with average C P U = 60 percent. Finally, test by accessing the ALB DNS name and verifying different hostnames on refresh; to trigger scaling, run C P U load on instances and observe ASG activity. screens.title: Instance Metadata vs User Data
screens.narratorSegment: Instance metadata and user data are complementary mechanisms for configuring EC2 instances. Instance metadata is a read-only data endpoint accessible from within the instance that exposes information such as the instance ID, AMI ID, public IP, and security groups. You can query it at a special address inside the instance, and it is useful for scripts that need to discover instance attributes at runtime. User data, by contrast, is a script or cloud-init payload supplied at launch and executed on first boot to configure the instance, install packages, or retrieve configuration from a central store. A concrete example: user data installs and configures the web server, while a startup script reads the metadata service to register the current instance ID with a configuration management system. Beware of leaking secrets in user data; instead grant the instance an IAM role and use identity to retrieve secrets securely. Another subtle point: metadata is only available from within the instance; do not assume external systems can query it. Use both features together for robust, automated instance configuration. Instance Metadata vs User Data means use user data to bootstrap instances at first boot and metadata for runtime discovery from inside the instance; avoid embedding secrets in either.. In practical terms, configure instances using runtime metadata and bootstrap scripts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Testing and Observability for ASGs
screens.narratorSegment: Testing an Auto Scaling design requires both functional validation and observability. Start by creating predictable traffic and observing CloudWatch metrics for C P U, network, and ELB request counts. Validate that new instances register with the ALB target group and only receive traffic after passing health checks. To simulate load, you might run a C P U stress tool on an instance in a staging environment to trigger the scaling policy. Watch the ASG lifecycle events to see launch and terminate actions and inspect system logs produced by user data to confirm proper bootstrapping. Common faults include misconfigured security groups that prevent instance registration, missing IAM permissions that block downloads in user data, and forgetting ELB health checks which leads to routing to unhealthy instances. Use CloudWatch Logs and ASG activity history to trace issues. When tuning, prefer smoothing evaluation periods and using target tracking for steady-state goals, reserving step policies for sudden, large spikes. Always test with both scale-out and scale-in scenarios so you avoid surprises in production. screens.title: When to combine Placement Groups and ELB/ASG
screens.narratorSegment: Combining placement groups with load balancing and autoscaling requires intentional design. Use a Cluster placement group when your application needs high inter-node bandwidth and low latency — common in HPC or in-memory distributed caches — and place those instances in the same Availability Zone. However, this optimizes for intra-AZ performance and reduces AZ redundancy, so pair it with cross-AZ load balancing or use separate ASGs per AZ to retain availability. Spread placement groups help protect single-instance critical services by placing instances on distinct hardware; they are useful for primary database nodes. Partition placement groups are a fit for large distributed systems that need isolation between partitions to limit blast radius during hardware failures. A frequent operational trade-off is that tightly packing instances can improve performance but increases AZ-level risk. When you need both resilience and performance, consider replicating the placement group pattern across multiple AZs or combining partition placement with multi-AZ replication. Always measure application latency and throughput with and without placement groups to justify the choice. Balance performance needs with availability goals

screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the main concepts to carry forward. Third, scaling policies determine how ASG changes capacity: use target tracking for steady goals, step scaling for graduated responses, and simple scaling for one-off thresholds. Fourth, placement groups let you influence physical hardware placement — cluster for performance, spread for failure isolation, partition for large distributed systems. Finally, instance metadata and user data let instances discover attributes at runtime and bootstrap themselves on first boot. Keep security and operational best practices in mind: avoid embedding secrets, configure health checks and cooldowns, and test scaling behavior under load. These are the practical building blocks you will apply in real deployments.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we unpack the practical tools AWS gives you to make EC2-based applications resilient and elastic. You will learn to pick the right load balancer for HTTP, TCP, or appliance workloads; to design Auto Scaling Groups that keep your application healthy while controlling cost; and to apply placement groups when low latency or hardware isolation matters. We'll also show how instance metadata and user data let you configure instances automatically during launch. Each concept is grounded in concrete examples you can replicate in the console: creating an Application Load Balancer for URL routing, using a launch template with user data to install a web server, and choosing target tracking scaling so your group maintains a C P U target without manual thresholds. A common trap is tuning too many static thresholds and forgetting cooldowns; we'll make that concrete. By the end you'll understand not just which service to choose, but why it matters for availability, performance, and operational simplicity. Consider how your current application would behave if one AZ failed — that question will guide the architecture choices on the upcoming screens.

These learning objectives map directly to the skills you'll practice. First, you will distinguish between Application, Network, and Gateway Load Balancers and pick the right one for real traffic patterns. Second, you'll design and create Auto Scaling Groups that specify launch templates, and desired/min/max capacities to keep applications available. Third, you'll configure scaling policies — simple, step, and target tracking — and understand when each fits operational needs. Lastly on this screen, you'll learn to use instance metadata and user data to automate instance bootstrapping. Each objective pairs a practical task with why it matters: picking the wrong balancer can bottleneck traffic; poorly tuned scaling produces cost and instability; and missing automation means slower, error-prone deployments. Throughout the exercises you'll see short console commands and configuration examples so you can apply these skills in a lab or production environment. Reflect on which objective will most change how you operate EC2 fleets, and keep that goal in mind as you move through the hands-on sections.

This second objectives slide expands the practical tasks you will perform and why they matter. You will create a launch template that includes AMI, instance type, security groups, and user data so new instances come online configured. You will attach an Auto Scaling Group to an Application Load Balancer and validate health checks so traffic routes only to healthy instances. You will apply target tracking to maintain an average C P U utilization and learn how step policies differ when you need aggressive scaling. Finally, you'll explore placement group variants — cluster, spread, and partition — and when each reduces latency or risk. These steps are intentionally procedural: building, observing, and tuning. The lab mirrors a real migration scenario where you need smooth autoscaling and quick recovery from instance failure. Keep an eye on cooldowns and health checks during your trials; they are common sources of instability if omitted or misconfigured.

Elastic Load Balancing is the front door for your application. At its core it distributes incoming traffic across multiple targets to increase fault tolerance and scalability. The Application Load Balancer operates at the application layer and is purpose-built for HTTP and HTTPS workloads. Use it when you need host-, path-, or header-based routing and when integrating with containers or microservices. The Network Load Balancer works at the transport layer for TCP, UDP, or TLS traffic and shines when extreme performance and static IP addresses are required. It is ideal for high-throughput, low-latency services. The Gateway Load Balancer is a specialized option for deploying third-party virtual appliances such as firewalls or intrusion detection systems; it helps insert and scale network appliances transparently. A common misconception is thinking ALB is always the best choice because it has advanced routing; instead match the layer and protocol to your workload. For example, a web application with URL-based routing and AWS WAF should use ALB. A high-frequency trading gateway requiring microsecond latency should consider NLB and placement of instances in a cluster placement group. Remember that the choice impacts routing, health checks, and how target registration works.

An Auto Scaling Group is a control plane construct that ensures a specified number of healthy EC2 instances are running. It automates instance lifecycle actions: launching new instances when demand increases or when health checks fail, and terminating instances when demand drops. To configure an ASG you provide a launch template that defines AMI, instance type, security groups, and user data. You also set desired, minimum, and maximum capacities so the group knows its safe operating window. ASGs integrate with CloudWatch alarms to trigger scaling actions and with load balancers to register targets and use ELB health checks. A practical example: set desired capacity to two and minimum to one so your application can tolerate a single instance failure while keeping cost under control. A misconception is treating ASG as purely reactive; with target tracking it behaves proactively to maintain metrics like average C P U. Proper health checks and cooldowns are essential; without them an ASG can rapidly spawn and kill instances, a condition called flapping. Think of ASG as an automated steward of your compute capacity. Auto Scaling Groups (ASG) means asg keeps a fleet at desired size and manages launches/terminations based on capacity and policy rules.. In practical terms, ensure availability by maintaining a desired fleet size. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A launch template centralizes the configuration that an ASG uses when launching EC2 instances. It includes the AMI, instance type, security groups, and user data. User data is a script executed during the first boot and is commonly used to install packages, start services, and render configuration files. This is essential for immutable infrastructure: every time an instance launches it runs the same bootstrap steps. For example, a user data script can install Nginx and write an index page that displays the instance hostname, making it easy to validate ELB routing. A common misconception is embedding secrets in user data; instead use IAM roles or a secrets service. In the visual code panel you'll see a sample user data script that updates the package manager, installs Nginx, enables the service, and writes a simple H T M L file with the instance's hostname. When building launch templates, pin AMI IDs to stable versions and keep security groups minimal for least privilege. This pattern enables automatic, consistent instance configuration and faster recovery when ASG replaces instances. Launch Templates & User Data means use a launch template with user data to ensure each instance boots into the same, production-ready state automatically.. In practical terms, automate instance setup at boot with reproducible templates. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Scaling policies define the rules an Auto Scaling Group follows when adjusting capacity. A simple scaling policy reacts to a single alarm: when a metric crosses a threshold, the ASG performs a fixed scaling action, such as adding two instances. Step scaling refines this by mapping different threshold ranges to different actions — for example, add one instance when C P U exceeds 60 percent, add three when it exceeds 80 percent. Target tracking is the most hands-off and commonly recommended approach: you pick a metric and a desired target, such as average C P U at 60 percent, and the ASG automatically adjusts capacity to maintain that target. This reduces manual tuning and complexity. However, target tracking requires choosing a metric that accurately reflects application load. Watch for flapping if you omit cooldowns or if your metric is noisy; step policies can be useful when you need aggressive responses to large spikes. A good practice is to use target tracking for steady-state metrics and step policies for predictable large-scale events. Always test in a staging environment and monitor CloudWatch metrics to validate policy behavior.

Auto Scaling reacts to CloudWatch alarms which observe metrics from instances and load balancers. An alarm evaluates a metric over a period and triggers scaling actions when a threshold is breached. Health checks belonging to ELB or EC2 ensure that instances that fail to respond are marked unhealthy and replaced. A typical flow: CloudWatch alarm detects sustained high C P U, ASG scales out by launching instances using the launch template, the new instances run user data and register with the target group, and ELB health checks confirm readiness before routing traffic. If you forget to use ELB health checks, the ASG may mark an instance healthy before it is actually serving traffic. Another failure mode is missing IAM permissions for instances to reach configuration endpoints or to fetch secrets, which prevents bootstrapping. When designing alarms, pick evaluation periods and datapoints that smooth short spikes and set cooldowns so new instances have time to initialize. This flow minimizes false positives and ensures scaling decisions are effective and safe. In practical terms, how alarms drive scaling actions and the role of health checks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Placement groups influence how EC2 instances are placed on underlying hardware to meet specific workload requirements. A Cluster placement group packs instances closely in a single Availability Zone to achieve low network latency and high throughput, which is valuable for high-performance computing. A Spread placement group distributes instances across distinct hardware to minimize correlated failures; each instance runs on different racks, making this a good choice for critical single-instance services like primary databases. Partition placement groups divide the fleet into partitions that isolate groups of instances from each other; instances in different partitions do not share underlying hardware, providing fault isolation useful for distributed systems like Cassandra, HDFS, or Kafka. A common misconception is that placement groups increase availability across AZs; they are confined to AZs, so you must combine them with multi-AZ architectures for full AZ-level resilience. Choose cluster for performance, spread for individual instance resilience, and partition for large distributed clusters needing partition-wise isolation. Validate that new instances register with the ALB target group and only receive traffic after passing health checks. To simulate load, you might run a C P U stress tool on an instance in a staging environment to trigger the scaling policy. Watch the ASG lifecycle events to see launch and terminate actions and inspect system logs produced by user data to confirm proper bootstrapping. Common faults include misconfigured security groups that prevent instance registration, missing IAM permissions that block downloads in user data, and forgetting ELB health checks which leads to routing to unhealthy instances. Use CloudWatch Logs and ASG activity history to trace issues. When tuning, prefer smoothing evaluation periods and using target tracking for steady-state goals, reserving step policies for sudden, large spikes. Always test with both scale-out and scale-in scenarios so you avoid surprises in production. Combining placement groups with load balancing and autoscaling requires intentional design. Use a Cluster placement group when your application needs high inter-node bandwidth and low latency — common in HPC or in-memory distributed caches — and place those instances in the same Availability Zone. However, this optimizes for intra-AZ performance and reduces AZ redundancy, so pair it with cross-AZ load balancing or use separate ASGs per AZ to retain availability. Spread placement groups help protect single-instance critical services by placing instances on distinct hardware; they are useful for primary database nodes. Partition placement groups are a fit for large distributed systems that need isolation between partitions to limit blast radius during hardware failures. A frequent operational trade-off is that tightly packing instances can improve performance but increases AZ-level risk. When you need both resilience and performance, consider replicating the placement group pattern across multiple AZs or combining partition placement with multi-AZ replication. Always measure application latency and throughput with and without placement groups to justify the choice. Let's summarize the main concepts to carry forward. First, Elastic Load Balancing automatically distributes traffic; choose ALB for Layer 7 routing and integration, NLB for Layer 4 performance, and GWLB to scale network appliances. Second, Auto Scaling Groups maintain a desired capacity and automate recovery; they use launch templates so new instances boot consistently. Third, scaling policies determine how ASG changes capacity: use target tracking for steady goals, step scaling for graduated responses, and simple scaling for one-off thresholds. Fourth, placement groups let you influence physical hardware placement — cluster for performance, spread for failure isolation, partition for large distributed systems. Finally, instance metadata and user data let instances discover attributes at runtime and bootstrap themselves on first boot. Keep security and operational best practices in mind: avoid embedding secrets, configure health checks and cooldowns, and test scaling behavior under load. These are the practical building blocks you will apply in real deployments.

A few quick memory aids help make operational decisions easier. Remember: ALB equals application layer routing and WAF integration; NLB equals high performance and static IPs; GWLB equals appliance insertion. For scaling, recall the pattern: simple equals single threshold, step equals graduated responses, and target tracking equals goal-oriented autoscaling. Use launch templates to make instances identical and user data to script first-boot configuration. Finally, place instances according to workload needs: cluster for performance, spread to reduce correlated failure, partition to isolate partitions of a large system. These compact rules help you make decisions during architecture reviews and incident response. Before you finalize a design, ask whether you have health checks, cooldowns, and monitoring in place — missing any of these is a frequent operational blind spot. Keep these checks in mind as you implement the lab and real deployments.
